right_to_work_note: South Dakota's right-to-work rule is written into the state constitution, so no worker can be made to join a union or pay union dues to keep a job.
public_bargaining_note: State and local public workers can form unions and bargain over pay, hours, and working conditions under the Public Employees' Unions law.
public_strike_note: No public worker in South Dakota may strike against the state, a city or county, or a public school, and strikers face a daily civil fine.
agency_name: South Dakota Department of Labor and Regulation
state_note: South Dakota is unusual in giving public workers full bargaining rights while also writing right-to-work into its constitution.

right_to_work_note: Tennessee law says no worker can be required to join a union or pay union dues as a condition of getting or keeping a job.
public_bargaining_note: Most public workers cannot bargain collectively, but teachers can use voluntary collaborative conferencing with their school board, and transit workers bargain under federal law.
public_strike_note: Strikes by public workers are prohibited in Tennessee.
agency_name: Tennessee Department of Labor and Workforce Development
legal_aid_name: Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands
state_note: Tennessee ended teacher collective bargaining in 2011 and replaced it with voluntary collaborative conferencing, which is not binding bargaining.

right_to_work_note: Texas law, backed by the state constitution, says no one can be denied a job because they do or do not belong to a union.
public_bargaining_note: Texas generally bans collective bargaining for public workers, but police officers and firefighters in some cities can bargain or meet and confer under separate laws.
public_strike_note: Public workers in Texas may not strike or take part in an organized work stoppage, and a striker loses civil service and reemployment rights.
state_note: Texas bans public-sector bargaining for most government workers, though police and firefighters in some cities are the exception.

right_to_work_note: Utah law says no worker can be required to join a union or pay union dues as a condition of getting or keeping a job.
public_bargaining_note: Utah public workers can bargain collectively, because the 2025 law that would have banned it was repealed by the Legislature in December 2025 before it ever took effect.
public_strike_note: Public school workers are barred from striking under Utah law, and no Utah law gives other public workers a right to strike.
state_note: Utah's 2025 ban on public-sector bargaining (HB 267) was repealed by the Legislature in December 2025 after voters collected over 250,000 signatures to put it on the ballot, so bargaining rights stand.

right_to_work_note: Vermont has no right-to-work law, so a union contract may require workers it covers to pay fees for bargaining and representation.
public_bargaining_note: State, town, city, and school workers in Vermont can form unions and bargain over pay, hours, and working conditions.
public_strike_note: State workers may not strike, but town and city workers may strike after fact-finding, as long as the strike would not endanger public health, safety, or welfare.
state_note: Vermont is one of the few states where some public workers can legally strike: town and city workers may strike after fact-finding, but state workers may not.

right_to_work_note: Virginia law says no worker can be required to join a union or pay union dues as a condition of getting or keeping a job.
public_bargaining_note: Since May 1, 2021, Virginia cities, counties, and towns may choose to let their workers bargain collectively, but they are not required to, and state workers still cannot bargain.
public_strike_note: Public workers in Virginia still have no right to strike, and a public worker who strikes can be fired.
agency_name: Virginia Department of Labor and Industry
state_note: Virginia banned public-sector bargaining for decades, then in 2021 let each city and county decide for itself whether to allow it.

right_to_work_note: Washington has no right-to-work law, so a union contract may require workers it covers to pay fees for bargaining and representation.
public_bargaining_note: Washington state and local public workers, including teachers, can form unions and bargain over pay, hours, and working conditions.
public_strike_note: Washington law gives public workers no right to strike, and a court can order a public-worker strike to stop.
agency_name: Washington State Department of Labor & Industries
state_note: Washington public workers can bargain freely, but the law gives them no right to strike, so teacher walkouts have no legal protection.

right_to_work_note: West Virginia's 2016 Workplace Freedom Act says no worker can be required to join a union or pay union dues as a condition of getting or keeping a job.
public_bargaining_note: West Virginia law gives public workers no right to bargain collectively, mediate, or arbitrate with their government employer.
public_strike_note: Any work stoppage or strike by West Virginia public workers is unlawful, and school workers who strike lose pay for each day out.
state_note: West Virginia law states plainly that public workers have no right to bargain collectively and that any public-employee strike is unlawful.

right_to_work_note: Wisconsin's 2015 right-to-work law says no worker can be required to join a union or pay union dues as a condition of getting or keeping a job.
public_bargaining_note: Under Act 10 from 2011, most Wisconsin public workers can bargain only over base wages, with raises capped at inflation, while police and firefighters are exempt from those limits.
public_strike_note: Wisconsin law expressly bans strikes by municipal workers, and a court can order a strike to stop at once.
state_note: Under Act 10, most Wisconsin public workers can bargain only over base wages, and their unions must win a recertification vote every year.

right_to_work_note: Wyoming has had a right-to-work law since 1963, so no worker can be required to join a union or pay union dues to keep a job.
public_bargaining_note: Firefighters are the only Wyoming public workers with a state law giving them the right to bargain collectively; there is no general bargaining law for other public workers.
public_strike_note: Wyoming law gives public workers no right to strike.
state_note: Wyoming is a right-to-work state, but firefighters are the only public workers with a state law giving them the right to bargain.
